svg.title: Stratifying haematuria: which kind, in which group, and how much the yield differs
svg.desc: Schematic: how much the yield of investigation differs between kinds of blood in the urine and between groups of people. The first panel gives the denominator after referral to urology: IDENTIFY, a prospective cohort across 26 countries and 110 hospitals that recruited 10,896 people, found a urinary tract cancer in 28.2 per cent after adjustment for age, type of haematuria, sex, smoking, hospital and country, with a 95 per cent confidence interval of 22.3 to 34.1. Bars from longest to shortest read bladder cancer 24.7 per cent (19.1 to 30.2), prostate cancer 1.75 per cent (1.32 to 2.18), upper tract urothelial carcinoma 1.14 per cent (0.77 to 1.52) and kidney cancer 1.05 per cent (0.80 to 1.29). The population label states that these were people aged sixteen and over, referred to secondary care with suspected urinary tract cancer and with no previous urological malignancy, and a warning box adds that this denominator is people already referred to secondary care - not everyone with blood in the urine and certainly not the general population, the denominator in primary care being an entirely different one. The second panel is which kind of blood: visible haematuria is the strongest single marker in the dataset, adjusted odds ratio 3.47, 95 per cent confidence interval 2.90 to 4.15, with a note that an odds ratio is a ratio of odds between two groups rather than a multiple of the probability. Three bars below give the absolute numbers from a prospective observational study of more than 3,500 people quoted by the guideline: visible haematuria 13.2 per cent, overall 10.0 per cent, microhaematuria only 3.1 per cent. The third panel is the dipstick: the guideline defines microhaematuria as more than three red blood cells per high-power field on microscopic evaluation of a single, properly collected specimen, and states that it should not be defined by a positive dipstick alone; two bars show that 20.3 per cent of 237 women with a positive dipstick had normal microscopy, and that only 26 per cent of 54 people referred on the dipstick alone were confirmed on microscopy; a note adds that anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment does not change the evaluation. The fourth panel is the axis of the figure: for the same microhaematuria, the malignancy rate in three validation studies across three risk groups. In the low or negligible risk group: the first study of 1,018 people, all of whom had cystoscopy and imaging, found 0 cancers among 218, that is 0 per cent; the second, of 15,779 people who all had cystoscopy, found 3 among 727, that is 0.4 per cent; the third, of 1,730 women, found 0 among 322, that is 0 per cent; and for this group the guideline recommends repeating the urine test within six months rather than going straight to cystoscopy. In the intermediate group: 14 cancers among 447, 3.1 per cent; 18 among 1,863, 1.0 per cent; and 0.2 per cent among 463 women; the recommendation is cystoscopy plus renal ultrasound. In the high-risk group: 20 cancers among 353, 5.7 per cent; 836 among 13,189, 6.3 per cent; and 1.3 per cent among 945 women; the recommendation is cystoscopy plus axial upper tract imaging, with multiphasic CT urography preferred where there is no contraindication. The same panel carries a hatched box crossed out and labelled "there is no scoring table in this figure": no boxes for age, pack-years or degree of haematuria and no total to add up, because the guideline itself concedes the system is imperfect - it groups the risk of urothelial cancer with that of other urological cancers while using risk factors that are chiefly those for bladder cancer. Beside it the other half is set down honestly: in the 1,018-person study 34 cancers were found in all, 3.3 per cent, and 32 of them, 94 per cent, were low-grade Ta; and investigating more has costs the guideline lists, namely the discomfort and infection risk of cystoscopy, contrast reactions, the possibility of radiation-induced cancer and false positives leading to further tests. The fifth panel is the cell for women, in two columns with a dashed rule between them labelled to say that both statements stand in the same document, that this figure does not reconcile them, and that there is no arrow and no equals sign between the columns. The left column is the gap in the pathway: from the first claim for haematuria to diagnosis, women waited 85.4 days on average against 73.6 days for men, P below 0.001; 17.3 per cent of women against 14.1 per cent of men waited longer than six months; the odds of being given a diagnosis of urinary tract infection were 2.32 (2.07 to 2.59) and the odds of undergoing abdominal or pelvic imaging 0.80 (0.71 to 0.89); the odds, women against men, of three or more GP consultations before referral were 2.31 (1.98 to 2.69) for bladder cancer, the strongest sex effect of the 24 cancers studied; and the survival gap quoted by the guideline is 73.3 per cent at five years in women against 78.2 per cent in men, with the wording "may be in part attributable to" delay in diagnosis. A source line records that the first set comes from United States claims data for 2004 to 2010, 5,416 men and 2,233 women, and the third from the 2010 National Cancer Patient Experience Survey in England, 41,299 people and 24 cancers. The right column is the 2025 amendment to the same guideline: the low-risk age threshold for women was relaxed from under fifty to under sixty and intermediate risk became sixty and over; it states that women should not be characterised as high risk on age alone; and the reason is that in the study of 1,730 women, 11 of the 13 cancers were in women aged sixty and over. The sixth panel is headed "leave it and it becomes advanced: that arrow is not on this figure". Four bars give adjusted hazard ratios from the SEER-Medicare study of 29,740 people, for diagnosis at nine months rather than within three: overall 1.34; after further adjustment for stage and grade 1.29; in the low-grade group 2.11; in the low-stage Ta or Tis group 2.02; a dashed reference line marks 1.0. The note explains that the effect is strongest in the two groups least likely to invade the muscle, which is the shape of unmeasured confounding, and that the guideline goes no further than saying these delays have been suggested to contribute to a 34 per cent increase in cancer-specific mortality. Below it a multicentre series of 1,384 newly diagnosed bladder cancers is added: 11.6 per cent of those presenting with microhaematuria were T2 or above against 17.9 per cent of those with visible haematuria, multivariable odds ratio 1.69 (1.05 to 2.71, P equals 0.03), but there was no difference in grade between the groups - a difference in the stage distribution of two groups at one moment in time, not what happens to one person who waits. The panel closes by noting that what does hold up going to get it checked this month are two other pillars: a quarter of this group turn out to have bladder cancer, and settling the question takes one clinic visit. The seventh panel is the cell with no blood in it: the three NICE referral thresholds - aged forty-five and over with unexplained visible haematuria without urinary tract infection; visible haematuria that persists or recurs after successful treatment of infection; aged sixty and over with unexplained non-visible haematuria and either dysuria or a raised white cell count - together with a pale box for considering a non-urgent referral in people aged sixty and over with recurrent or persistent and unexplained urinary tract infection. Alongside, the European guideline notes that carcinoma in situ might be suspected in patients with lower urinary tract symptoms, especially irritative voiding symptoms, and the American guideline asks for the urine to be examined again after treatment where haematuria was attributed to infection. The eighth panel sets out the first round of tests in three columns: cystoscopy, done where symptoms suggest bladder cancer, with biopsy where needed, and which cannot be replaced by cytology or any other non-invasive test; upper tract imaging, the initial work-up using renal and bladder ultrasound and/or CT urography, with ultrasound unable to exclude upper tract urothelial carcinoma and unable to replace CT urography; and urine cytology, an adjunct to cystoscopy with a sensitivity of 84 per cent for high-grade or G3 tumours and only 16 per cent for low-grade or G1, a negative result excluding nothing, and a specimen of at least 25 mL of fresh urine required, first morning urine being unsuitable. A dashed box below records that this cell is not a general rule: "once a bladder tumour is seen, CT urography must follow" is not what the guideline says - the sentence is that CT urography should be performed in selected cases, for example tumours in the trigone or multiple or high-risk tumours, because the incidence of upper tract tumours in people with a bladder tumour is only 1.8 per cent, rising to 7.5 per cent for the trigone. At the foot of the figure is the Taiwanese section: the National Health Insurance fee schedule lists 28019C, cystoscopy, at 1,800 points and 15001C, body fluid cytology, at 480 points with urine included in the description; a full-text search for "CT urography" returns nothing, so there is no line item to find and the billing office or case manager has to be asked, with nothing inferred either way; the catastrophic illness certificate is valid for five years; and no official statistics exist for the cancer detection rate of haematuria clinics in Taiwan.

g.text: WHICH KIND OF HAEMATURIA, IN WHICH GROUP,
AND HOW MUCH THE YIELD DIFFERS
Which kind of blood, in
which group: the yield
differs a great deal
This figure answers one question only: in different
populations, and for different kinds of blood in the
urine, what proportion of people investigated turn out
to have a cancer. Every cell carries its denominator -
change the denominator and the number changes.
There is no arrow here from delay to stage, and no
table you can tick your way through. Which group you
are placed in is a judgement your doctor makes from
your circumstances as a whole; the question you can
ask out loud is "which group am I in, and on what
grounds".
The denominator after referral to urology
IDENTIFY is a prospective cohort across 26 countries and 110 hospitals
that recruited 10,896 people.
Cancers found in this group, after adjustment
Bladder cancer
95% confidence interval 19.1-30.2
Prostate cancer
Upper tract urothelial carcinoma
Kidney cancer
Urinary tract cancer of any kind: 28.2% (95% confidence
interval 22.3-34.1)
Population: aged sixteen and over, referred to secondary care with
suspected urinary tract cancer, with no previous urological malignancy;
adjusted for age, type of haematuria, sex, smoking, hospital and country. A
confidence interval, in plain words, is the range the answer would
probably fall in if the same study were run many times over.
The denominator has to be stated first
These are people already referred to secondary care - not
everyone with blood in the urine, and certainly not the general
population. In primary care the denominator is an entirely
different one.
Which kind of blood: within the same
group, the visible kind carries the most
weight
Visible haematuria is the strongest single marker in this
dataset
Adjusted odds ratio 3.47
95% confidence interval 2.90-4.15. An odds ratio is a ratio of odds
between two groups, not a multiple of the probability.
The absolute numbers read more easily (a prospective
observational study of more than 3,500 people, quoted by the
AUA/SUFU guideline)
Visible haematuria
Overall
Microhaematuria only
Three denominators from one study: this is the proportion in whom a
urinary tract cancer was found, not a statement of what blood in the urine
does to you.
The red square on the dipstick is not yet
haematuria
The guideline definition is unusually firm
More than three red blood cells per high-power field on
microscopic evaluation of a single, properly collected urine
specimen - and, in as many words, microhaematuria should not be
defined by a positive dipstick alone. A positive dipstick is only a
reason to do the microscopy.
Women with a positive dipstick whose microscopy was normal
237 women with a positive dipstick
Referrals made on the dipstick alone that were confirmed on
microscopy
54 people referred on the dipstick alone
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment does not change this: the guideline
asks for the same evaluation regardless of the type or level of therapy.
The same microhaematuria: how much the
yield differs between groups
Three validation studies, three risk groups, set side by side. This is not a
table to tick your way through.
Low or negligible risk
First study: 1,018 people, all had cystoscopy and imaging
218 in the low-risk group, 0 cancers
Second study: 15,779 people, all had cystoscopy
727 in the low-risk group, 3 cancers
Third study: 1,730 women
322 in the low-risk group, 0 cancers
The guideline recommends repeating the urine test within six
months, rather than going straight to cystoscopy.
Intermediate risk
First study: 1,018 people
447 at intermediate risk, 14 cancers
Second study: 15,779 people
1,863 at intermediate risk, 18 cancers
Third study: 1,730 women
463 at intermediate risk
The guideline recommends cystoscopy plus renal ultrasound.
High risk
First study: 1,018 people
353 at high risk, 20 cancers
Second study: 15,779 people
13,189 at high risk, 836 cancers
Third study: 1,730 women
945 at high risk
The guideline recommends cystoscopy plus axial upper tract
imaging, with multiphasic CT urography preferred where there is
no contraindication.
There is no scoring table in this figure
No boxes for age, pack-years or degree of haematuria, and no total
to add up. The guideline itself concedes that the system is
imperfect: it groups the risk of urothelial cancer together with that
of other urological cancers, while the risk factors it uses are
chiefly those for bladder cancer.
The other half belongs here too
In the 1,018-person study, 34 cancers were found in all (3.3%),
and 32 of them (94%) were low-grade Ta.
Investigating more has its own costs, which the guideline lists:
the discomfort and infection risk of cystoscopy, contrast
reactions, the possibility of radiation-induced cancer, and false
positives that lead to further tests.
For women, the same guideline says two
opposite things
On one side: a gap in the pathway (observational data)
From the first claim for haematuria to diagnosis
women 85.4 days on average, men 73.6 days (P<0.001)
Proportion taking longer than six months
women 17.3%, men 14.1%
Odds of being given a diagnosis of urinary tract infection
Odds of undergoing abdominal or pelvic imaging
Odds, women against men, of three or more GP consultations
before referral
bladder cancer 2.31 (1.98-2.69), the strongest sex effect of the 24
cancers studied
Survival gap quoted by the guideline
five-year survival 73.3% in women against 78.2% in men, with the
wording "may be in part attributable to" delay in diagnosis
The first set comes from United States claims data (2004 to 2010; 5,416
men and 2,233 women, all of whom first presented with haematuria and
were later diagnosed with bladder cancer); the third from the 2010
National Cancer Patient Experience Survey in England (41,299 people, 24
cancers).
No arrow, no equals sign
On the other side: the 2025 amendment to the same guideline
The low-risk age threshold for women was relaxed from under
fifty to under sixty, and intermediate risk became sixty and
over.
It states in as many words that women should not be
characterised as high risk on the basis of age alone.
The reason is the study of 1,730 women, in which 11 of the 13
cancers were in women aged sixty and over.
Both stand in the same document; this figure does not reconcile them - no
arrow between the two columns, and no equals sign
"Leave it and it becomes advanced": that
arrow is not on this figure
Not because it is frightening, but because the shape of the data does not
support it.
SEER-Medicare, 29,740 people: adjusted hazard ratio for
bladder cancer death when diagnosis came at nine months
rather than within three
Overall
After further adjustment for stage and grade
In the low-grade group
In the low-stage Ta / Tis group
The effect is strongest in the two groups least likely to invade the
muscle. A mechanism that really worked by giving the tumour time
to grow downwards would not be most visible there - this is the
shape of unmeasured confounding. The guideline's own wording
goes no further than saying these delays "have been suggested to
contribute to" a 34% increase in cancer-specific mortality.
A multicentre series of 1,384 newly diagnosed bladder cancers is
often misread in the same way: 11.6% of those presenting with
microhaematuria were T2 or above, against 17.9% of those with
visible haematuria, multivariable odds ratio 1.69 (1.05-2.71,
P=0.03) - but there was no difference in grade between the two
groups. That is a difference in the stage distribution of two groups
at one moment in time, not what happens to one person who waits.
What does hold up "go and get it checked this month" are two
other pillars: a quarter of this group turn out to have bladder
cancer, and settling the question takes one clinic visit. Neither
pillar needs to frighten anyone.
The cell with no blood in it is not empty
either
The NICE referral thresholds, word for word
Aged forty-five and over with unexplained visible haematuria
without urinary tract infection.
Visible haematuria that persists or recurs after successful
treatment of urinary tract infection.
Aged sixty and over with unexplained non-visible haematuria and
either dysuria or a raised white cell count on a blood test.
And one further cell: consider a non-urgent referral for people
aged sixty and over with recurrent or persistent and
unexplained urinary tract infection.
The European guideline is direct: carcinoma in situ "might be
suspected in patients with lower urinary tract symptoms,
especially irritative voiding symptoms". Frequency, urgency and
burning treated as cystitis month after month is what this cell
usually looks like.
The corresponding rule in the American guideline: where
haematuria has been attributed to a urinary tract infection, the
urine should be examined again after treatment to confirm that the
blood has gone.
What the first round of tests involves, and
which of them is not for everybody
Cystoscopy
Cystoscopy, with biopsy where needed, in people with symptoms
suggestive of bladder cancer.
The guideline sentence: it cannot be replaced by cytology or by
any other non-invasive test.
Upper tract imaging
The initial work-up uses renal and bladder ultrasound and/or CT
urography.
Ultrasound cannot exclude upper tract urothelial carcinoma and
cannot replace CT urography.
Urine cytology
An adjunct to cystoscopy, used to pick up high-grade tumours.
Sensitivity is 84% for high-grade / G3 tumours and only 16% for
low-grade / G1; a negative result does not exclude anything.
The specimen needs at least 25 mL of fresh urine; first morning
urine is not suitable.
This cell is not a general rule
"Once a bladder tumour is seen, CT urography must follow"
is not what the guideline says. The sentence reads: once a
bladder tumour has been detected, perform CT urography in
selected cases - for example tumours in the trigone, or
multiple or high-risk tumours. The reason is that the
incidence of upper tract tumours in people with a bladder
tumour is only 1.8%, rising to 7.5% for the trigone.
In Taiwan: what can be looked up, and what cannot
The National Health Insurance fee schedule lists 28019C,
cystoscopy, at 1,800 points.
Urine cytology is billed as 15001C, body fluid cytology, at 480
points; the description includes urine.
A full-text search of the fee schedule for "CT urography"
returns nothing at all - there is no line item to find, so how it is
billed and whether anything is payable has to be asked of the
hospital's billing office or your case manager. Nothing is
inferred either way.
For catastrophic illness registration, bladder cancer falls under
"other malignant tumours" within "cancers requiring active or
long-term treatment", and the certificate is valid for five years.
No official statistics exist for the cancer detection rate of
haematuria clinics in Taiwan - every proportion above belongs
to somebody else's population.
Schematic, redrawn from the IDENTIFY study (Khadhouri 2021), the
AUA/SUFU microhaematuria guideline (published 2020, amended
2025) and Barocas 2025, the EAU 2026 guideline on
non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer, NICE NG12, Cohn 2014,
Lyratzopoulos 2012, Hollenbeck 2010, Ramirez 2016 and the
Taiwanese National Health Insurance fee schedule; not reproduced
from the figures of the original papers. The cohorts, designs and
endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data points must not
be compared directly.
